data.name: Caloric restriction
data.description: Reduced caloric intake without malnutrition; associated with lifespan extension across species.
data.description_beginner: Eating meaningfully fewer calories without becoming malnourished. It's linked to longer lifespan across many species and is one of the classic ways researchers dial down mTOR signaling through diet.

studies.title: Caloric restriction improves health and survival of rhesus monkeys

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Direct comparison of two long-term primate CR studies (NIA, Wisconsin) supports consistent health benefits; the survival effect depended on study design and control-diet composition.

studies.title: Safety of two-year caloric restriction in non-obese healthy individuals
studies.authors: Romashkan SV; Ravussin E et al.

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Two years of sustained 25% caloric restriction in healthy non-obese adults was safe overall, though it lowered bone density more than controls.

studies.title: 4E-BP extends lifespan upon dietary restriction by enhancing mitochondrial activity in Drosophila
studies.authors: Zid BM; Rogers AN; Katewa SD; Vargas MA; Kolipinski MC; Lu TA; Benzer S; Kapahi P

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Connected the dots between diet, mTOR, and lifespan. 4E-BP, an mTOR target, is upregulated on dietary restriction and here was shown to be REQUIRED for the lifespan boost, working by selectively boosting translation of mitochondrial genes. A rare case pinning a specific mTOR effector to the longevity benefit of eating less.

studies.title: Extending healthy life span--from yeast to humans
studies.authors: Fontana L; Partridge L; Longo VD

evidence.label: Review — secondary literature, not a new result
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Influential review proposing that dietary restriction and reduced nutrient-sensing signalling (mTOR, GH/IGF-1) may slow ageing through similar, evolutionarily conserved mechanisms. Lifespan extension is shown in yeast, invertebrates, rodents and rhesus monkeys; in humans the evidence is limited to protective biomarker changes and genetic associations.

studies.title: Anticipatory metabolic regulation drives the distinct and improved metabolic state of caloric restriction compared to Fasting-Refeeding cycles.
studies.authors: Velingkaar N; Astafev AA; Prabahar A; Maravillas MA; Trokhimenko E; Rom JB; Asi GJ; Piontkivska H; Jiang P; Kondratov RV

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Comparing caloric restriction (CR, one meal/day) to a fasting-refeeding-fasting (FRF) regimen with matched food intake and fasting duration, CR engages anticipatory, circadian-clock-aligned metabolic control (hepatic mTOR signaling, ketogenesis, metabolic gene coordination), whereas FRF responses track direct nutrient/gastric-emptying cues and disrupt circadian rhythmicity. CR improved glucose and fatty-acid metabolism; FRF caused glucose intolerance and hepatic fat accumulation.

studies.title: A role for autophagy in the extension of lifespan by dietary restriction in C. elegans
studies.authors: Hansen M; Chandra A; Mitic LL; Onken B; Driscoll M; Kenyon C

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Makes autophagy a necessary step between dietary restriction and a longer life, not a side effect of it: blocking autophagy genes abolishes the lifespan extension produced both by dietary restriction and by TOR inhibition. The paper is equally careful about what autophagy cannot do on its own, because autophagy still runs in animals lacking DAF-16/FOXO and yet those animals are not long-lived. Boundary: worms; necessity was shown, sufficiency was not.

studies.title: Redox activation of ATG5 licenses autophagy upon nutrient restriction
studies.authors: Shin S; Korobkina ED; Lennicke C; Burger N; Zhang B; Xiao H; Wang Y; Petrocelli JJ; Wei SM; Wood D; Lei Y; Zhang X; Perez-Matos MC; Sharif MA; Zhang J; Cochemé HM; Mair WB; Chouchani ET

evidence.label: Preprint, not peer-reviewed
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.model_system: Human cell lines and mice; tissue-resolved cysteine redox proteomics (OxiDR atlas) under dietary restriction
studies.finding: Dietary restriction selectively oxidizes a specific, tissue-resolved set of cysteines rather than oxidizing the proteome broadly. One of the most strongly oxidized is Cys19 on the core autophagy protein ATG5; this oxidation is required for ATG5 to bind ATG10 and form the ATG5-ATG12 conjugate that lipidates LC3B and builds the autophagosome. In mice lacking this redox switch, nutrient restriction fails to trigger autophagy, causing severe tissue pathology and early death -- a single oxidized cysteine gates the autophagic response to fasting.
